# Worked answers

[]{#sol-da-normal-ten} **[Ten normal observations](#ex-da-normal-ten).**

The sample mean is $4.642$ and the bias-corrected sample standard deviation is $1.306$. Then

$$
4.642\pm 2.262\times\frac{1.306}{\sqrt{10}}=4.642\pm 0.935,
$$

which is $(3.71,\,5.58)$.

[]{#sol-da-melbourne-oil} **[Household spending on fuel](#ex-da-melbourne-oil).**

$$
1136\pm 2.678\times\frac{178}{\sqrt{51}}=1136\pm 66.8,
$$

which is $(1069.2,\,1202.8)$.

[]{#sol-da-pilot-width} **[Narrowing a pilot interval](#ex-da-pilot-width).**

The pilot half-width is $(82.5-59.3)/2=11.6$ kg at $n=100$. The margin scales as $1/\sqrt n$, so a margin of 1 kg needs

$$
n\ge 100\times 11.6^2=13456.
$$

Recovering the pilot standard deviation with a $t_{99}$ quantile near $1.98$ and then planning the new interval with $z_{0.975}=1.96$ lowers the requirement to $13188$. Either figure is a sample of more than thirteen thousand.

[]{#sol-da-paper-thickness} **[Printer paper](#ex-da-paper-thickness).**

The mean is $101$ and the bias-corrected standard deviation is $3.916$. Then

$$
101\pm 2.262\times\frac{3.916}{\sqrt{10}}=101\pm 2.80,
$$

which is $(98.2,\,103.8)$, matching $(98.1,\,103.9)$ at the rounding of $s$. The interval contains 100, so these ten sheets do not show that the mean thickness differs from the advertised value.

[]{#sol-da-sleep-sample-size} **[Hours of sleep](#ex-da-sleep-sample-size).**

The pilot margin is $7.39=t_{3,\,0.975}\,s/\sqrt{4}$ with $t_{3,\,0.975}\approx 3.182$, so $s\approx 4.65$. A future sample of size $n$ has margin $t_{n-1,\,0.975}\,s/\sqrt n$. The smallest $n$ for which this is at most 2 is $n=24$: $t_{23,\,0.975}\approx 2.07$ and $2.07\times 4.65/\sqrt{24}\approx 1.96<2$, while $n=23$ is just over 2.

[]{#sol-da-shady-poll} **[A difference of proportions](#ex-da-shady-poll).**

$\widehat p_W=350/980=0.3571$ and $\widehat p_M=420/1108=0.3791$. The difference is $-0.0219$ and the estimated standard error is $0.0211$. Then

$$
-0.0219\pm 1.645\times 0.0211=(-0.057,\,0.013).
$$

[]{#sol-da-juice-variance} **[Variance of a fill volume](#ex-da-juice-variance).**

$(n-1)s^2=26\times 5.86^2=893.0$. The interval is

$$
\left(\frac{893.0}{41.92},\,\frac{893.0}{13.84}\right)=(21.3,\,64.5).
$$

[]{#sol-da-caffeine-cola} **[Caffeine in a cola](#ex-da-caffeine-cola).**

The model is an independent normal sample. The hypotheses are $H_0:\mu=19$ against $H_1:\mu>19$. The statistic $(\overline X-19)/(s/\sqrt n)$ is $t_{39}$ under $H_0$. The observed value is

$$
\frac{19.57-19}{1.40/\sqrt{40}}=2.57.
$$

The one-sided p-value is 0.007, so $H_0$ is rejected at level 0.05. The mean caffeine in this brand is higher than 19 mg per serving.

[]{#sol-da-brexit-poll} **[A later poll on leaving](#ex-da-brexit-poll).**

$H_0:p=0.519$ against $H_1:p\neq 0.519$. The observed leave proportion is 0.46. The statistic $z=-2.64$ has two-sided p-value about 0.0082, so the poll is not consistent with an unchanged leave proportion at level 0.05. An approximate 95% interval for the leave proportion is $(0.42,\,0.50)$.

[]{#sol-da-steel-rods} **[Steel rod diameters](#ex-da-steel-rods).**

(a) $(6-6.1)/0.1=-1$, and $\Phi(-1)=0.1587$, about 0.159.

(b) The 0.01 quantile of a normal law sits $2.326$ standard deviations below the mean, so the mean must be $6+2.326\times 0.1=6.23$ cm.

(c) $t=(6.1-6)/(0.1/\sqrt{100})=10$ on 99 degrees of freedom. The one-sided p-value is negligible, so the mean diameter is greater than 6 cm.

[]{#sol-da-shuffle} **[A shuffling machine](#ex-da-shuffle).**

$H_0:p=1/2$ against $H_1:p>1/2$, with $X\sim\Bin(20,p)$ the number of red top cards. The observed value is 17. The p-value $\Pr(X\ge 17\mid p=1/2)=0.00174$, so the machine is not consistent with a fair top card.

[]{#sol-da-two-proportions} **[Two proportions](#ex-da-two-proportions).**

$H_0:p_X=p_Y$ against $H_1:p_X>p_Y$. The p-value 0.23 does not reject at level 0.05. The interval $(-0.067,\,0.121)$ contains 0, which is the same conclusion.

[]{#sol-da-home-ground} **[Home-ground wins](#ex-da-home-ground).**

$H_0$ is equal home and away win probabilities. $H_1$ is that they differ. The p-value 0.2526 does not reject equality at level 0.05. These games do not show a home-ground advantage.

[]{#sol-da-sickle-anova} **[Haemoglobin and sickle-cell type](#ex-da-sickle-anova).**

$H_0$ is equal mean haemoglobin in the three disease types. $H_1$ is that the means are not all equal. The degrees of freedom are $3-1=2$ and $41-3=38$. The $F$ statistic is

$$
F=\frac{99.89/2}{1.00}=49.95.
$$

The p-value is about $2.3\times 10^{-11}$, so the means differ at level 0.05. The $F$ test assumes independent normal observations with a common variance.

[]{#sol-da-bonferroni} **[Five treatments, ten pairs](#ex-da-bonferroni).**

Each of the 10 pairs is tested at level $0.05/10=0.005$.

[]{#sol-da-pine-trees} **[Height and age of pine trees](#ex-da-pine-trees).**

The fitted line is $\widehat{\mathrm{height}}=5.599+3.395\times\mathrm{age}$. At age 4 the prediction is $5.599+3.3949\times 4=19.18$ metres. The slope's p-value is far below 0.05, so the fit shows a linear association between age and height.

[]{#sol-da-birth-weight} **[Birth weight and mother's age](#ex-da-birth-weight).**

At age 15 the fitted mean is $3204.23-18.84\times 15=2921$ g. At age 35 it is $3204.23-18.84\times 35=2544$ g. The slope's p-value is 0.1102, so the decrease is not distinguishable from zero at level 0.05.

[]{#sol-da-orange-yield} **[Rain, food, and orange yield](#ex-da-orange-yield).**

$$
99.504+0.01763\times 1000+0.04020\times 500=137.3
$$

kilograms. A prediction interval covers a new tree, which still has variance $\sigma^2$ even if the mean yield were known. A confidence interval covers only the mean, so it is shorter.

[]{#sol-da-shark-swim} **[How far sharks swim](#ex-da-shark-swim).**

(a) The margin scales as $1/\sqrt n$. Cutting it by four multiplies the sample size by 16, so $151\times 16=2416$ females.

(b) $H_0$ is equal mean weights. The two-sided alternative is that the means differ. The p-value 0.00164 rejects equality at level 0.05.

(c) A 100 kg female is predicted to swim $2.631+0.0937\times 100=12.0$ km. A 100 kg male is predicted to swim $12.0-1.966=10.0$ km.

[]{#sol-da-isotopia-wages} **[Wages, class, and gender](#ex-da-isotopia-wages).**

(a) A working-class man is estimated at $93.242-4.247=88.995$, about 89 thousand dollars.

(b) The coefficient 3.927 is the estimated difference, in thousands of dollars, between women and men of the same class. The sign says women are estimated higher.

(c) The gender row has p-value 0.01029, so the difference is distinguishable from zero at level 0.05. The gender mean square is $3194/1$ and the residual mean square is 102, so $F=3194/102=31.3$, which is the square of the $t$ statistic and gives the same conclusion.

[]{#sol-da-possums} **[Possums in five areas](#ex-da-possums).**

The total is 1380, so each expected count is $1380/5=276$. The Pearson statistic is

$$
\sum\frac{(O_i-276)^2}{276}=15.63.
$$

The approximate null distribution is $\chi^2_4$. The p-value 0.0036 rejects equal attractiveness at level 0.05. Some areas are preferred.

[]{#sol-da-fruit-flies} **[Genotype and mating success](#ex-da-fruit-flies).**

Row totals are 12, 29 and 9. Column totals are 23 and 27. The grand total is 50. Expected counts are the products of the margins divided by 50:

| | No | Yes |
|---|---:|---:|
| AA | 5.52 | 6.48 |
| AB | 13.34 | 15.66 |
| BB | 4.14 | 4.86 |

The p-value 0.2853 does not reject independence at level 0.05. These trials do not show an association between genotype and mating success.
